cover.hook: A 27-billion-parameter AI agent just outperformed Anthropic's and OpenAI's flagship models at a real research task - the same week OpenAI promised zero data retention on those flagship models and a new study found a third of the web has been written by AI since ChatGPT launched.
cover.sub: Also this week: a procurement software company cut its product launch time 68 percent using OpenAI's agents, and new spending data shows OpenAI closing the gap with Anthropic among paying businesses.

items.title: A procurement software company cut its product launch time 68 percent using OpenAI's agents
items.body: Stampli used OpenAI's Codex and ChatGPT Work to turn an estimated 243 hours of launch production - blog posts, launch emails, a webinar, social creative, a press release - into about 77 hours for its new Deep Finance product. The team went from an early prototype to a public launch in roughly six weeks.
items.tease: Next: a 27-billion-parameter AI agent just outperformed Anthropic and OpenAI's flagship models at a scientific task.
items.reelLine: A procurement software company, Stampli, cut its product launch time 68 percent using OpenAI's Codex and ChatGPT Work.

items.title: A 27-billion-parameter AI agent just outperformed Anthropic's and OpenAI's flagship models at reproducing scientific research
items.body: Inherent, a London AI lab founded by DeepMind alumni, says its agent Faraday - built on a comparatively small 27-billion-parameter model called Qwen 3.6 - outperformed Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8 and OpenAI's GPT-5.5 at independently reproducing the findings of published research papers without being told the answer first. The lab says it was testing for 'research taste': an instinct for which experiments are worth running.
items.tease: Next: OpenAI just promised something it's never fully guaranteed before - zero data retention across its most powerful models.
items.reelLine: A 27-billion-parameter AI agent from London startup Inherent outperformed Anthropic and OpenAI's flagship models at reproducing published research.

items.title: OpenAI reaffirmed it won't retain your data on its frontier models - and previewed a way to catch misuse without reading your prompts
items.body: Under OpenAI's Zero Data Retention commitment for eligible API customers, prompts and outputs aren't kept after a request is processed, aren't reviewed by staff, and aren't used to train future models unless a customer opts in. A new system called Private Safety Processing is meant to let automated checks flag a risk category across related activity without giving OpenAI personnel access to the actual content.
items.tease: Next: a new study says a third of the web published since ChatGPT launched shows signs of being written by AI.
items.reelLine: OpenAI reaffirmed zero data retention for its frontier models and previewed Private Safety Processing, a way to flag misuse without staff reading customer prompts.

items.title: A third of web pages published since ChatGPT launched show signs of being written by AI
items.body: A Pew Research study used the Common Crawl archive and Open Pangram's detection tool to check nearly half a million English-language pages from the past five years. Pages on .com domains showed signs of AI authorship at roughly ten times the rate of .edu or .gov pages - both around 1 percent - while .org domains came in near 4.6 percent. Pew and TechCrunch both cautioned that AI-detection tools aren't infallible and can misflag human writing.
items.tease: Next: new spending data shows OpenAI closing the gap with Anthropic among paying business users.
items.reelLine: A Pew Research study finds a third of web pages published since ChatGPT launched show signs of AI authorship, with .com domains far ahead of .edu and .gov.

items.title: OpenAI is closing the gap with Anthropic among paying business users
items.body: Spending data from Ramp, tracking over 70,000 U.S. businesses, shows 43.5 percent paid for Anthropic subscriptions or tokens in July, versus 39.7 percent for OpenAI - but OpenAI has been growing faster than Anthropic so far this quarter. Anthropic's newest model, Fable 5, made up only 6 percent of its business token volume, which Ramp partly attributes to its price - roughly double OpenAI's comparable GPT-5.6 Sol.
items.reelLine: New Ramp spending data shows OpenAI closing the gap with Anthropic among paying U.S. business users, growing faster this quarter.

cover.hook: Canada's flagship R&D funding program has a stream built specifically for AI adoption and development
cover.sub: NRC IRAP's AI Assist stream pairs a financial contribution with a dedicated advisor - confirm eligibility with an NRC Industrial Technology Advisor before applying.

posts.detailChip: NRC IRAP - Industrial Research Assistance Program
posts.title: Who it's for and how it works
posts.body: NRC IRAP is Canada's flagship innovation funding program for SMEs developing and commercializing technology products or services, combining a financial contribution for R&D with advice from a dedicated NRC Industrial Technology Advisor. Streams include Core, AI Assist, and Clean Technology. It's open to incorporated, for-profit Canadian companies with up to 500 full-time employees pursuing technology-driven innovation with commercialization potential - sole proprietorships, partnerships, and co-operatives don't qualify, and neither do projects without a path to market. Intake is continuous, but the first step is contacting an Industrial Technology Advisor rather than submitting a standard application form.

why.title: Why it matters
why.body: IRAP doesn't publish a fixed grant amount because contributions are scoped individually with an advisor rather than set by a formula. That's a different kind of program than a fixed grant - the advisor helps shape the project itself, which can matter as much as the funding for a business without in-house R&D planning experience, and the AI Assist stream exists specifically for companies building or adapting AI.

posts.detailChip: Enterprise AI adoption - NVIDIA and ChatGPT Work
posts.title: What changed and why it matters
posts.body: NVIDIA has rolled ChatGPT Work across go-to-market teams, solutions architects, event planning, and engineering. Event prep for its GTC conference used to mean building account lists and tracking registrations by hand in spreadsheets; solutions architects use it to connect fast-moving external developments to internal priorities; and one engineer described moving from idea to working prototype in about 3 to 5 days, versus an estimated 2 to 3 weeks building the same components manually across separate tools.

why.title: Why it matters for a small operation
why.body: Most of the visible AI news is model-versus-model. What's actually changing how teams spend their time is using AI to compress the ordinary busywork - assembling lists, prepping for an event, pulling together scattered information - into hours instead of weeks. That's the same category of task most small operations already do by hand.

cover.hook: OpenAI just promised it won't keep your prompts or your data on its most powerful models - here's how to actually check whether any AI vendor is telling you the truth
cover.sub: Zero data retention isn't unique to OpenAI. It's a real setting or contract term you can ask for and verify before you connect a tool to anything sensitive.

posts.detailChip: Checking an AI vendor's data policy
posts.title: How to actually use it
posts.body: Before connecting an AI tool to client records, health information, or financial data, ask the vendor four direct questions: does zero data retention (or an equivalent) actually apply to your plan tier, since it's often reserved for paid or enterprise accounts rather than the free version; what happens to your data if you don't explicitly opt in to model training, and is that the default or something you have to turn off; can you get the answer in writing, as a data processing agreement or a terms addendum, rather than a verbal answer from a sales rep; and what does the vendor's own safety monitoring still see, since even a strong data-retention promise can come with automated checks running in the background.

why.title: Why it matters
why.body: A business handling sensitive records doesn't need to avoid AI tools - it needs answers to these questions before it connects one. The same week OpenAI made its zero-retention promise public, it also had to explain what its own safety systems still monitor and why. That trade-off exists with every AI vendor, whether or not they say so upfront.

cover.hook: 4 things worth doing now that a third of the web has been written by AI since ChatGPT launched
cover.sub: Not a reason to panic about AI content - a reason to change a few default habits.

list.title: Ask your writer or agency directly
list.body: If someone else writes for your business - a freelancer, an agency, a content service - ask exactly how much of it is AI-drafted and how much is edited by a person. Not to shame the tool, to know what you're actually paying for.

list.title: Judge content on accuracy, not on who wrote it
list.body: AI-written and human-written aren't the same axis as accurate and inaccurate. A generic AI draft can be wrong; so can a rushed human one. Check the claims, not the authorship.

list.title: Weight primary sources higher than you used to
list.body: A Pew Research study found .com content shows signs of AI authorship at roughly ten times the rate of .edu or .gov content. A blog post repeating a claim is worth less than it used to be - go closer to the original source before you repeat something.

list.title: Decide on purpose where your own content needs a human voice
list.body: Some of what a business publishes - a policy explanation, a customer email, a local story - loses something if it reads like everyone else's AI draft. Decide deliberately where that matters to you, instead of by default.

why.title: Why it matters
why.body: None of this is about avoiding AI in content - it's about not treating 'someone wrote this' as proof of anything anymore. The businesses handling this well are being explicit about where AI helps, not pretending it isn't happening.

cover.hook: A Thunder Bay company that's been fixing phones and networks since 1985 brought AI safety cameras to the world's biggest mining convention
cover.sub: Teleco demonstrated AI-powered PPE detection and thermal imaging built for mine sites at PDAC 2026, inside FedNor's Northern Ontario pavilion.

posts.detailChip: Teleco - AI safety cameras for mine sites
posts.title: What they did
posts.body: Teleco has operated in Thunder Bay since 1985 as a managed IT and communications services provider. In March 2026, FedNor selected Teleco as one of seven exhibitors in the Northern Ontario Mining Showcase pavilion at PDAC in Toronto - the world's largest mineral exploration and mining convention - where the company demonstrated AI-powered PPE detection cameras, thermal imaging systems, and portable camera solutions built for active mine sites, aimed at improving hazard awareness, strengthening compliance, and supporting safety decision-making underground and on the surface.

why.title: Why it matters
why.body: This is a local IT company extending decades of infrastructure work into AI-based safety hardware for the region's dominant industry, rather than adopting AI as a generic office tool. FedNor has run the NOMS pavilion since 2015, and participating Northern Ontario businesses have generated more than $100 million in sales and exports and more than 900 jobs through the program - a real bridge from local expertise to a global stage.

cover.hook: Anthropic just posted jobs for a Compute Country Lead and a Community Engagement Manager based in Alberta - and it still hasn't announced a single Canadian project
cover.sub: Where the next wave of AI infrastructure gets built decides where the jobs, power contracts, and local investment show up - and Northwestern Ontario isn't automatically part of that conversation.

posts.title: The infrastructure decisions are the ones that actually matter here
posts.body: BetaKit reported Anthropic is hiring a Compute Country Lead 'ultimately responsible for bringing gigawatts of compute online in Canada' - working with staff in both Canada and the U.S. to find and lease sites, secure power, finance projects, oversee construction, and lobby federal and provincial governments - alongside a Data Centre Community Engagement Manager based in Alberta to liaise with municipal officials, local organizations, and residents near prospective sites. Anthropic confirmed the postings but hasn't announced a project, site, investment, or timeline - this is the earliest possible stage.

why.title: Why it matters here
why.body: Most AI news that reaches Northwestern Ontario is about a model release or a feature update - something you can try or ignore. This is a different category: a decision about where the jobs and power contracts behind gigawatts of AI compute actually get built in Canada. Alberta is where the postings point right now, not the Northwest - but the criteria a lab uses to pick a site, like power availability and a willing local government, are exactly what regional economic development groups can influence before a company like Anthropic locks in a location. Watching this stage, not just the eventual announcement, is where the leverage is.
